paper_title: On the Tip of the Tongue: First-Token Cueing as a Behavioral Probe of Recall Failures in LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. We study this with First-Token Cueing, a behavioral probe that prefills the response with the first token of the gold answer. Model uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, where it already predicts correctness, and among gold prefixes of any length the first token alone accounts for the largest share of recovered errors. Across 16 open models, this one token corrects between a fifth and a half of the errors on multi-token answers in English QA and improves accuracy in all seven languages of a multilingual benchmark. Most of the errors it corrects are also solved by the model's own sampled reasoning, a criterion for encoded knowledge, and models recognize correct starts they do not produce: they continue a correct start more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability, yet rarely find it without the gold answer. These results locate a recoverable class of factual errors at the first decoding step, where inference-time methods may gain the most.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) acquire substantial factual knowledge during pretraining (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020), yet they still make factual errors in closed-book question answering (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). The usual remedy, scaling parameters and data (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), treats these errors as missing knowledge. Recent work suggests that many of * Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Phonemic cueing in human tip-of-the-tongue states (left; Brown and McNeill, 1966; James and Burke, 2000) and First-Token Cueing in LLMs (right). In both, production fails at the start of the answer, and supplying its first unit, phoneme or token, lets the speaker or the model complete it. them are failures of recall instead: probes recover correct answers from internal states when the generated answer is wrong (Burns et al., 2023; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Orgad et al., 2025), lightweight interventions can surface such knowledge (Li et al., 2023; Simhi et al., 2024), and models encode many facts they do not verbalize (Gekhman et al., 2025; Calderon et al., 2026). Where in generation these failures arise is less clear. The first answer token is natural place to look. In autoregressive generation, each token is conditioned on the ones before it, so an early commitment shapes the rest of the answer. The first token of hallucinated span carries the strongest error signal (Snel and Oh, 2025), and answer commitment localizes to the first decoding step (Yeom et al., 2026). These studies read the first token as signal of error. Whether supplying the correct first token resolves the error has not been tested. Human memory offers parallel. In the tip-ofthe-tongue (TOT) state, speaker cannot produce word they know, yet can often report its meaning and parts of its form, such as its first letter (Brown and McNeill, 1966; Schwartz and Metcalfe, 2011). The transmission deficit hypothesis attributes this to weak connection between an available meaning and its sound form, not to missing knowledge (Burke et al., 1991). TOT states are often resolved by partial cue, most effectively the first sound of the word (Meyer and Bock, 1992; Rastle and Burke, 1996; James and Burke, 2000), in line with encoding specificity: cue helps to the extent that it matches the stored target (Tulving and Thomson, 1973). In this account the cue completes access to word the speaker already has, rather than supplying the word (Figure 1). We take this paradigm as motivating analogy, not as claim of shared mechanism, and ask behavioral question: how many closed-book errors of LLMs are resolved by supplying the start of the answer? First-Token Cueing prefills the models response with the first token of the gold answer and lets the model continue. If many errors are failures of recall, cue this small should resolve large share of them. Because the cue comes from the gold answer, First-Token Cueing measures which errors are recoverable rather than fixing them at inference time. The cue also carries information about the answer, so we call errors it corrects cue-recoverable and test whether they are recall failures in the sense of prior work, failures to produce an answer the model encodes. Our central claim is that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. Three findings across 16 open models from three families support this claim. First, the failure is located at the first token: uncertainty about correctness concentrates there, and the first token accounts for the largest share of the errors that gold prefixes recover. Second, the first token recovers many errors: on multi-token answers it corrects between fifth and half of baseline errors in every model on the English benchmarks and improves accuracy in every language of multilingual benchmark, while random, incorrect, and generic prefixes do not help. Third, models recognize correct starts they do not produce: when the correct start lies outside the models own top candidates, models continue it more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability, yet search over first characters without the gold answer gains little because the model prefers its own wrong start.

sections.title: These results locate a recoverable class of factual
sections.content: errors at the first decoding step and suggest that inference-time methods should concentrate there. Our contributions are: We show that uncertainty about correctness concentrates at the first answer token, and that the first token accounts for the largest share of what gold prefixes recover (Sections 3 and 5.4). We show that supplying only the gold first token corrects large share of errors across 16 models and seven languages, and describe how this share varies with scale, language, and tokenizer (Section 5). We introduce crossed-cue control that separates recognition from the information carried by cue, and show that models can recognize correct answer starts that they fail to produce, but rarely find them on their own (Section 6).

sections.title: LLMs
sections.content: LLMs store many facts in their parameters (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020), but recall is skewed toward popular facts (Kandpal et al., 2023; Mallen et al., 2023) and asymmetric across the direction of relation (Berglund et al., 2024). Several lines of work find that models hold more than they produce. Probes read the correct answer from internal states when the output is wrong (Burns et al., 2023; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Orgad et al., 2025), and inference-time interventions on these states surface it (Li et al., 2023; Simhi et al., 2024). Gekhman et al. (2025) measure knowledge as how often model scores correct answer above an incorrect one and find correct answers that the model ranks first yet fails to generate even with extensive sampling; Calderon et al. (2026) find that recall rather than encoding limits frontier models. Our probe is behavioral and needs only prefilling. Instead of scoring complete answers, it supplies only the first token, so the model must produce the rest of the answer itself, and our crossed-cue control compares the correct start with incorrect starts of the same answer type and prior probability.

sections.title: Generation
sections.content: Early tokens shape the rest of autoregressive generation. The first token of hallucinated span car2 ries the strongest uncertainty signal (Snel and Oh, 2025), answer commitment localizes to the first decoding step and errors often reflect probability mass spread over surface forms (Yeom et al., 2026), and first-token entropy predicts the difficulty of reasoning step (Zeng et al., 2026). These studies use the first token as signal; we intervene on it. Branching at the first decoding step, by continuing each of the most probable first tokens greedily, uncovers reasoning paths that greedy decoding misses (Wang and Zhou, 2024); our first-token oracle (Section 6.1) applies this branching to factual answers. prefilled start also commits the model: prefilling few tokens of compliant response is enough to bypass safety alignment (Qi et al., 2025), and output prefilling has been used to steer the first token in multiple-choice evaluation (Cappelletti et al., 2025). Such generic prefix carries no information about the answer and, in our open-ended setting, does not help (Section 5.2).

sections.title: Memory
sections.content: TOT states were described as early as James (1890) and have been studied experimentally since Brown and McNeill (1966); Schwartz and Metcalfe (2011) review the field. Models of lexical access separate retrieving words meaning from retrieving its form (Dell, 1986; Levelt et al., 1999), which the transmission deficit hypothesis uses to explain TOT states (Burke et al., 1991). Feeling-of-knowing judgments show that people recognize information they cannot produce (Hart, 1965), the human counterpart of the recognition we test in Section 6. We adopt the onset-cue paradigm (Meyer and Bock, 1992; Rastle and Burke, 1996; James and Burke, 2000) as behavioral test for LLMs. Unlike phoneme, token can span several characters or whole word, so first-token cue can carry more of the answer than an onset (Section 5.3).

sections.title: Token
sections.content: If closed-book errors are failures to start the answer, uncertainty should peak at the first answer token, and the first token should carry most of the signal about whether the answer will be correct. Speech production suggests the same: phonological encoding proceeds left to right (Levelt, 1989; Levelt et al., 1999), and in TOT states retrieval stalls at the onset (Brown and McNeill, 1966; Burke et al., 1991). 3 Figure 2: Uncertainty localizes to the first token. AUROC and PRR (left) and mean entropy (right) by answertoken position for Llama-3.1 8B on TriviaQA. The first token has the highest entropy, and its entropy predicts correctness nearly as well as the average over the whole answer. Setup. We first examine Llama-3.1 8B on TriviaQA (closed-book, greedy decoding). At each position of the generated answer we compute the entropy of the next-token distribution, and we compare the first three positions with the average over all answer tokens. We measure how well each separates correct from incorrect answers with AUROC and with the Prediction Rejection Ratio (PRR; Malinin and Gales, 2021), which compares the accuracy gained by rejecting the most uncertain answers with that of an oracle (1: oracle, 0: random). Uncertainty peaks at the first token. Entropy is highest at the first token and drops sharply afterwards (Figure 2). Lower entropy at later positions is expected, since the start of an answer constrains its continuation. The informative result is that first-token entropy alone separates correct from incorrect answers nearly as well as the wholeanswer average, while the second and third tokens do much worse: the signal about correctness is already present when the model chooses how to start. First-token entropy predicts errors in every model. For all 16 models, first-token entropy predicts whether the Baseline answer is correct, with AUROC between about 0.6 and 0.85 on the English benchmarks (Appendix I). The first-step distribution also predicts which errors the cue recovers (Section 5): the cue fixes about two-thirds of the errors in which the gold first token was the models second to fifth choice, and under third of those in which it ranked below the top thousand. Answer generation thus appears to divide into two steps: at the first token the model selects an answer, under high uncertainty that predicts correctness, and at later tokens it completes the answer under strong constraint from the prefix. First-Token Cueing intervenes at the first step.

sections.title: Do Not Produce
sections.content: The gold first token corrects many errors, but it also carries information about the answer: told that the host city of the 1900 Olympics starts with P, one can guess Paris without knowing the fact. We first relate the recovered errors to what the model produces without cue (Section 6.1). Many are errors in which the model proposed the correct start but committed to another, or which its own sampled reasoning also solves, so the cue often selects an answer the model can reach on its own. We then test the information account directly (Section 6.2). If the cue acted only as information, the model would continue an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability as confidently as the correct one. It does not, although it rarely finds the correct start without the gold answer. Unless stated otherwise, we use questions whose gold answer has at least two tokens.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Using First-Token Cueing, behavioral probe modeled on onset cueing in tip-of-the-tongue states, we find that many closed-book errors of 16 open models are first-token recall failures. Uncertainty about correctness concentrates at the first answer token. Supplying only that token corrects large share of errors on multi-token answers, in every model on every benchmark and language we tested, and accounts for the largest share of what longer gold prefixes recover. The errors it corrects are mostly ones the models own sampled reasoning also solves, and the recoveries go beyond the information in the cue: when the correct start lies outside the models candidates, the model continues it more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability. These errors are failures to start an answer that the model can complete and recognize once started. The results suggest where inference-time methods should spend computation: these errors are decided at the first answer token, whereas decoding and test-time scaling treat every step alike. Because confidence favors the correct start over an incorrect one of similar prior probability but not over the models own preferred start (Section 6.2), choosing among starts will need evidence from outside the model, such as retrieval, which can also supply starts outside the models candidates. Whether such methods recover the gains of First-Token Cueing without the gold answer remains open.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We study short-answer factual QA, where the gold answer and its first token are well defined, which makes the first token precise target for behavioral probe. Extending the probe to long-form generation, where the counterpart would be the first token of each factual claim, is natural next step. First-Token Cueing is diagnostic rather than decoding method: it uses the gold answer to measure how many errors the first token resolves. Accordingly, we identify recall failures behaviorally, through cue recovery and its overlap with reasoning-based recovery, rather than from internal states. Supplying the first token without the gold answer, for example from retrieval, is direction for future work.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Broader impact. sections.title: A Experimental Details
sections.content: A.1 Datasets Table 3 summarizes the datasets used in this study. All datasets are loaded through the HuggingFace datasets library, except MKQA, which is read from local JSONL file. For NQ-Open and WebQuestions, each item provides list of acceptable answers; we treat the first entry as the gold answer and the remainder as aliases A(y). For TriviaQA and MKQA, the provided alias list is used directly. For MKQA, samples whose answer string for the target language is empty are filtered out. A.2 Models and Inference Backend We evaluate 16 open-weight instruction-tuned models from three dense-Transformer families: five Gemma-3 models (270M, 1B, 4B, 12B, and 27B parameters), seven Qwen-2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B, and 72B), and four Llama models spanning two generations (Llama-3.2 at 1B and 3B; Llama-3.1 at 8B and 70B). All checkpoints are the official HuggingFace -Instruct (Qwen, Llama) or -it (Gemma) variants. All models are served with vLLM on single NVIDIA B200 GPU (no tensor parallelism), using context window of 4,096 tokens, bfloat16 precision, and GPU memory utilization tuned per model around 0.9. For each model, prompts are wrapped in the models native chat template with generationprompt marker appended, so that all inputs are tokenized in the models expected chat format rather than as raw text. A.3 Decoding Hyperparameters We compare six conditions that vary along two axes: prompt (direct-answer vs. chain-of-thought) and decoding (greedy vs. sampling). Table 4 summarizes the hyperparameters. Baseline and First-Token Cueing share the same decoding policy (greedy, 50-token budget) and the direct-answer prompt; they differ only in whether the gold answers first token is prepended to the assistant response. Greedy CoT uses the CoT prompt with greedy decoding and 1,024-token budget to accommodate the reasoning trace. The three sampling conditions all use temperature 0.7 and topp = 0.95 with = 16 generations per question: pass@16 (Direct sampling) uses the direct-answer prompt with 50-token budget; pass@k (CoT sampling) (k {4, 16}) uses the CoT prompt with 1,024-token budget and shares single = 16 sample pool, with pass@k computed via the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. (2021). A.4 Prompt Templates Direct-answer prompt. Used by Baseline, FirstToken Cueing, and pass@16 (Direct sampling). fixed system message (Prompt 1) is followed by five fixed user/assistant demonstrations, with the current question appended as the final user turn. Applying Φ() to this message sequence yields the prefix xq. Prompt 1: Direct-answer System Prompt Answer the question directly. Provide only the exact answer without any explanation or conversational filler. CoT prompt. Used by Greedy CoT, pass@4 (CoT sampling), and pass@16 (CoT sampling). Zero-shot chain-of-thought with no demonstrations. Prompt 2: CoT System Prompt You are careful and logical thinker. First, think step-by-step about the question. After your reasoning, you must conclude your response on new line with the exact phrase: The answer is [your exact short answer]. The short answer is extracted from the models full output by case-insensitive matching of the phrase the answer is, allowing optional whitespace and separator characters (colon, hyphen, or asterisk) before the answer span, with the remainder captured as the parsed answer. On parsing failure, the full output is still forwarded to the judge model, marked as [Parsing Failed]. A.5 LLM-as-Judge All responses are graded by single judge model, gpt-oss-120b, served with vLLM in eagerexecution mode with chunked prefill disabled, context window of 4,096 tokens, and GPU memory utilization set to 0.80. Decoding is greedy. The judge system prompt is given in Prompt 3, with condition-specific user prompts in Prompts 4 and 5.

sections.content: A first token carries different amount of information depending on the tokenizer and the script: it may be whole word, subword, single character, or an informative entity fragment. We quantify how much of the answer the first token carries under each tokenizer and script. Across tokenizers. On the English benchmarks, the mean gold first token has 3.84, 3.16, and 3.06 characters under the Gemma-3, Llama-3, and Qwen-2.5 tokenizers, and 2031% of questions receive single-character first token  (Table 19)  . Stratifying the cueing gain by first-token length  (Table 18)  , all 64 (model, length) cells are positive, so the effect is present even when the cue is single character. The gain grows with the length of the cue in the same way under all three tokenizers, and the 4+-character bucket is the largest for every model. more informative cue thus yields larger Across languages. Tokenizer effects are much larger across the seven MKQA languages (Figure 5 and Table 20). In the non-Latin scripts (RU, AR, JA, ZH, KO), 3894% of first tokens are single character, and answers span more tokens (4.96.5 vs. 3.64.7 for EN and ES), so the = 1 cue covers smaller fraction of the answer. Prefilling the gold answers first character as single-character token breaks the tokenization the model expects: with this naive prefill, Llama-3.1 8B loses 13.0, 7.1, and 7.8pp of judge accuracy on TriviaQA, NQ-Open, and WebQuestions, often switching to an entity whose canonical first token is single letter (e.g., George Carlin Gore Vidal). Constraining the first token to tokens that begin with the character avoids this and raises EM by +10.5pp instead  (Table 22)  . Results. Selecting by total log-probability gains +2.1pp, slightly less than beam search (+3.0pp), although the candidate set contains correct answer for 64.2% of questions. Selecting by continuation confidence alone fixes more errors when the greedy first character is wrong (+8.4pp) but abandons correct answers elsewhere (4.4pp overall). On questions whose greedy first character is wrong, the correct-character continuation has lower mean entropy than the median of the other 35 continuations in 82.7% of questions, but lower than the continuation of the models own (wrong) character in only 39.9%. The model can thus distinguish correct start from arbitrary alternatives, but not from the start it already prefers. Between two starts of equal prior probability, its confidence favors the correct one (Section 6.2); among many starts that include its own preferred one, the preferred start usually wins. sections.content: For each of the 16 models, we compute the firststep distribution of every question in the three English QA benchmarks with vLLM, using the top1,000 log-probabilities plus uniform tail for the remaining mass; for Llama-3.1 8B this approximation agrees with the exact entropy at Pearson = 0.999. The recomputed greedy first token matches the stored Baseline output in 9699% of questions (83% for Llama-3.2 1B, whose chat template inserts the current date). Table 23 reports the AUROC with which firsttoken entropy predicts whether the Baseline answer is correct. Table 24 groups Baseline errors by the rank of the gold first token: recovery falls from 65.5% when the gold token was ranked 2nd5th to 30.3% beyond rank 1,000.
